opus-5.5.text:
I think what I find really compelling about Peter's setup is that it's a glimpse of where the workflow is heading, even if it's a bit ahead of where most people are comfortable today. He'll have a whole bank of agents running at once, each one off on its own task, and his role shifts from writing code to something more like directing traffic. He's checking in, reviewing diffs, nudging one agent that went down the wrong path, kicking off a new task on another. It's less "programmer at a keyboard" and more like a manager, or almost like a conductor.

What appeals to me is that it takes seriously the fact that these models are now good enough to do meaningful chunks of work autonomously, but not so good that you can just walk away. So the bottleneck moves. It's no longer how fast you can type or even how fast a single agent can work. It's how fast *you* can verify, how well you can decompose a problem into pieces that can run in parallel without stepping on each other, and how quickly you can context-switch. That's a genuinely new skill, and I think people underestimate how different it is from traditional programming.

I'll say I'm personally still a bit more conservative. I like to keep things on a tighter leash, work in smaller increments, actually read the code, because these models still make weird mistakes, and if you let five of them run wild you can accumulate a lot of slop very quickly. But I respect that Peter is pushing on the frontier and finding out what actually works. Somebody has to figure out the ergonomics of this, and he's clearly building real intuitions about how far you can push it. I think a lot of us will end up somewhere closer to his style as the models get more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response mentions agents handling autonomous chunks of work, but does not identify whole features as the larger unit of action.

r002.rationale: It describes agents working on separate tasks in parallel and says to decompose work so the pieces can proceed without stepping on each other.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what's compelling about it is that he's basically treating the agents the way you'd treat a team, not a tool. Most people still use these things as a very fancy autocomplete: you have one agent, you give it a task, you babysit it, you wait. Peter's doing something closer to being an engineering manager. He's got several of them going at once, each in its own worktree or branch, each with a scoped task, and his job shifts from writing code to writing good specs and reviewing the output.

That shift is the interesting part to me, because it changes where the bottleneck is. The bottleneck is no longer typing speed or even thinking speed on any one problem. It becomes: how well can you decompose work into chunks that are independent enough to parallelize, and how fast can you verify what comes back. Those are genuinely different skills from traditional programming, and I think a lot of people haven't internalized that yet.

The other thing I like is that it's honest about the failure modes. He's not pretending the agents are infallible. He's saying, look, each one is going to be wrong some fraction of the time, so you want many attempts, cheap to discard, and you want strong tests and clear acceptance criteria so you can tell quickly which ones to keep. It's kind of a Monte Carlo approach to software engineering. You accept variance and you build the harness around it.

And it fits something I've been noticing in my own workflow, which is that the limiting resource is increasingly my attention, not the model's capability. So anything that lets me amortize my attention across more concurrent work is a real multiplier. I don't think we have the tooling right yet, the UX for juggling five agents is still pretty clunky, but the direction feels correct.

r001.rationale: The response describes scoped tasks and independent chunks, but does not identify whole features as the larger unit delegated to agents.

r002.rationale: It says several agents work in parallel on independent, scoped tasks, but does not clearly identify that work as noninterfering feature work.

astra-6.text:
What appeals to me is the shift from writing all the code yourself to setting up work that agents can do independently. You can have several things moving at once, and your job becomes deciding what to ask for, giving enough context, and checking whether the result actually makes sense.

The interesting constraint is your own attention. Spinning up more agents doesn’t automatically make you more productive, because now you have more output to review and more changes to integrate. So the skill is figuring out how to divide the work and how to verify it efficiently. I find that a really interesting way of programming: you’re still responsible for the software, but you’re operating at a different level.

r001.rationale: The response describes delegating independent work generally, but does not identify whole features as the larger unit of work.

r002.rationale: It says several things can proceed at once and mentions dividing work, but does not specify assigning noninterfering feature work to separate agents.

sol-6.1.text: What appeals to me is the shift from writing every line of code yourself to setting up the work so that agents can make progress independently. You’re deciding what to delegate, giving enough context, and then reviewing what comes back. With multiple agents, the bottleneck becomes your attention: can you keep track of what they’re doing and evaluate the results? I like that framing because it makes the human’s role very concrete. You still need taste and technical judgment, but you’re applying them at a different level.
